notes: Crown Prosecution Service judicial review; Keene LJ quashes refusal of joint trial of alternative summary charges.

enrichment.short_title: CPS v Blaydon Youth Court: joint trial of alternative summary charges
key_facts: A 17-year-old youth faced two alternative informations for the same events: racially aggravated section 4A Public Order Act 1986 and the basic section 4A offence.
Blaydon Youth Court refused a joint trial, treating the informations as duplicitous under Rule 12 and requiring the prosecutor to elect between them.
The defence remained neutral on a joint trial and the defendant did not appear on the judicial review.
The Crown Prosecution Service sought judicial review after Leveson J granted permission.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of a magistrates' youth court decision refusing to try alternative summary charges jointly.
enrichment.outcome: The youth court decision was quashed as based on a misunderstanding of Rule 12 and perverse; the court ordered a joint trial of both informations.
enrichment.ratio: Magistrates' courts may try separate alternative informations together where it is in the interests of justice; Rule 12 addresses duplicity within a single information only, and conviction on a more serious alternative does not require conviction on the lesser charge where adjournment sine die, nominal sentence or absolute discharge is available.
legal_issues: Whether Rule 12 prevents joint trial of alternative informations
Whether magistrates must convict on both charges if they convict on the racially aggravated offence
Whether absence of a magistrates' court equivalent to section 6(3) Criminal Law Act 1967 bars joint trial
Whether joint trial of alternative charges is perverse where facts and witnesses are the same

notes: Father-and-son agricultural labour fraud sentence appeal; seven-year terms upheld.

enrichment.short_title: R v Cox: appeal against seven-year sentences for agricultural immigration fraud
key_facts: Victor Cox and his son Jayson Cox ran companies supplying temporary agricultural workers to contractors on terms that all workers would be legally entitled to work in the UK.
Workers were largely overseas nationals not entitled to work; forged immigration papers were supplied and bogus Lithuanian work-permit applications were submitted under a training scheme.

Following a four-month trial at Canterbury Crown Court the appellants were convicted of conspiracy to defraud, conspiracy to use false instruments and two counts of conspiracy to facilitate illegal entry.
Each received seven years' imprisonment concurrently on all counts and eight-year director disqualification.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against sentence by leave of the single judge after conviction on four conspiracy counts.
enrichment.outcome: Appeals dismissed; seven-year sentences were severe but not manifestly excessive and equal treatment of father and son was justified.
enrichment.ratio: Large-scale persistent immigration and contract fraud exploiting vulnerable workers, continuing after bail and motivated by greed, may properly attract a seven-year deterrent sentence even for defendants of previous good character; director disqualification for eight years was within the sentencing judge's discretion.
legal_issues: Whether seven-year concurrent sentences were manifestly excessive
Whether the son should have received a lower sentence than the prime mover father
Whether eight-year director disqualification was too long
Relevance of workers' voluntary arrival and proper treatment to sentence

notes: Short permission judgment in Sri Lankan asylum judicial review; section 94 certified claim.

enrichment.short_title: Mylvaganam: permission to challenge Sri Lanka removal certification
key_facts: The applicant arrived using a forged passport and did not claim asylum immediately.
The Secretary of State rejected the asylum claim in a detailed decision letter dated 30 July 2004 and certified the claim under section 94.
The applicant contended he could not safely be removed to parts of Sri Lanka given his profile as a high-profile Tamil not supporting the LTTE.
Procedural unfairness was rejected; the applicant was on bail at the permission hearing.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Permission application in judicial review of a section 94 certified asylum refusal.
enrichment.outcome: Permission granted on the safety-of-removal point only; procedural unfairness refused; expedition directed for substantive hearing with costs reserved.
enrichment.ratio: Even where an applicant's entry history is unimpressive and procedural fairness points fail, permission may be granted where the decision letter may not adequately address whether removal to particular parts of Sri Lanka is safe for a claimant alleging high-profile Tamil political status.
legal_issues: Whether the decision letter adequately addressed safe removal to parts of Sri Lanka
Whether section 94 certification was procedurally unfair
Construction of section 94 in light of Thangarasa
Whether the claim should proceed to a full hearing or adjudicator
linked_authorities: Thangarasa v Secretary of State for the Home Department

notes: Neighbour dispute trial on roadway easements, trespass and wayleave damages; lengthy Chancery judgment.

enrichment.short_title: Perlman v Rayden: St John's Wood neighbour easement and trespass dispute
key_facts: George Perlman of 6A Elm Tree Road and Paul and Claire Rayden of No 6 disputed rights over a shared cul-de-sac roadway serving three St John's Wood houses near Lord's Cricket Ground.
The Raydens carried out front elevation works, installed lights and a dormer, and built a rear extension encroaching on Perlman's rights of access.
Perlman claimed trespass, nuisance and breach of easement, seeking declarations, injunctions and wayleave-based damages.
The rear extension was later demolished; Perlman revoked informal parking consent in October 2002.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Trial of two related Chancery actions for declarations, injunctions and damages arising from neighbour building works and use of a shared private roadway.
enrichment.outcome: Perlman largely succeeded on liability; wayleave damages of £10,000 were awarded for certain roadway uses, further damages followed for access interference, declarations were made about future building gaps, and £5,000 aggravated damages were awarded.
enrichment.ratio: Easement rights must be exercised without exceeding the grant; use of a dominant owner's roadway for building works and installations without consent gives rise to wayleave damages, and a rights-suspension covenant may operate despite casual prior consent where covenants are breached; aggravated damages may compensate mental distress where defendants persistently denied wrongdoing.
legal_issues: Construction of express grants of right of way and ancillary repair rights
Whether Raydens' works constituted trespass or permissible easement exercise
Operation of a covenant suspending rights for non-compliance with covenants
Assessment of damages on the wayleave principle and availability of aggravated damages

notes: Supplemental Preston equal-pay appeal ruling; Secretary of State denied costs and leave refused.

enrichment.short_title: Powerhouse v Seeboard: interested party costs and leave in Preston equal pay litigation
key_facts: The appeal formed part of the Preston litigation involving thousands of equal pay claims by part-time workers.
The Secretary of State for Education and Skills intervened as interested party after falling out of the proceedings as employer in the test case.
Successful appellants were entitled to costs against respondents; the Secretary of State sought his costs too.
The court had already handed down judgment on the substantive equal pay point.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Post-judgment applications on costs for an interested party and for leave to appeal to the House of Lords.
enrichment.outcome: The Secretary of State's costs application was refused and leave to appeal was refused; appellants' costs against respondents were not disputed.
enrichment.ratio: An interested party who is not a party and whose submissions largely duplicate those of successful appellants is not ordinarily entitled to costs; even had the Secretary of State been a party, two sets of costs would rarely be justified where representation overlapped, following Bolton principles.
legal_issues: Whether a successful interested party may recover costs
Application of Bolton to duplicate representation in test litigation
Whether the equal pay point warranted leapfrog leave to the House of Lords

notes: Landmark ASBO publicity judicial review; Kennedy LJ dismisses Article 8 challenge to Brent leaflet campaign.

enrichment.short_title: R v Metropolitan Police Commissioner: lawfulness of ASBO publicity leaflets
key_facts: Three young men subject to anti-social behaviour orders at Brill House, Brent challenged publicity after a 15-day magistrates' hearing.
On 2 October 2003 Brent Council and the Metropolitan Police distributed leaflets with photographs, names, ages and details of ASBOs across a wide area.
Publicity also appeared on the council website and in tenant newsletter Partnership News following serious persistent anti-social behaviour.
Claimants sought declarations that the publicity was unlawful and damages for breach of Article 8 ECHR.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of post-ASBO publicity by a local authority and police, with the Secretary of State as interested party.
enrichment.outcome: Applications dismissed; publicity including photographs and personal details was necessary and proportionate to enforce orders, restore confidence and inform victims, though future decision-makers must expressly consider Convention rights.
enrichment.ratio: ASBO publicity may engage Article 8 but effective enforcement and community reassurance ordinarily require names, photographs and partial addresses; publicity need not be confined to geographic exclusion zones where orders contain wider association and behaviour restrictions, provided aims are identified and measures are proportionate rather than mere naming and shaming.
legal_issues: Whether post-ASBO publicity infringed Article 8 private life
Whether publicity was necessary and proportionate to legitimate aims
Implied power to publicise ASBOs under the Crime and Disorder Act 1998
Whether distribution beyond exclusion zones and use of PACE photographs was lawful

notes: Restricted patient conditional discharge challenge; Collins J upholds tribunal on Thornford Park deprivation of liberty.

enrichment.short_title: R (G) v MHRT: conditional discharge and deprivation of liberty at Thornford Park
key_facts: G, a 67-year-old restricted Broadmoor patient detained since 1967 for serious sexual violence, had stable paranoid schizophrenia and improved behaviour at Thornford Park.
A tribunal deferred conditional discharge in July 2003 requiring hostel residence and supervision, but no suitable hostel could be found.
The tribunal reconsidered the case and would revoke the provisional conditional discharge because Thornford Park conditions could not be fulfilled.
G sought discharge with a condition requiring continued residence at Thornford Park under substantially the same secure regime.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of a Mental Health Review Tribunal decision refusing conditional discharge where proposed residence conditions could not be implemented.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; requiring residence at Thornford Park on the existing restrictive regime would amount to continued deprivation of liberty and was beyond the tribunal's power.
enrichment.ratio: A tribunal may treat a deferred conditional discharge as provisional and reconsider it when arrangements cannot be implemented, following R (H); conditional discharge cannot lawfully impose conditions that leave a patient in the same secure hospital regime as detention, and patient consent cannot convert continuing deprivation of liberty into voluntary status conferring tribunal jurisdiction.
legal_issues: Whether proposed Thornford Park residence conditions constituted deprivation of liberty or mere restriction on movement
Tribunal power to reconsider deferred conditional discharge when hostel placement fails
Application of PH and Ashingdane to conditional discharge conditions
Whether consent could permit conditional discharge while remaining in hospital detention

notes: Out-of-time costs appeal in Shirburn Castle occupancy litigation; disclosure point fails.

enrichment.short_title: Macclesfield v Beechwood: out-of-time appeal against no-order costs decision
key_facts: The 9th Earl of Macclesfield litigated his right to occupy Shirburn Castle against Beechwood Estates Company.
Lewison J held the Earl occupied on a contractual licence requiring two years' notice rather than a life interest by proprietary estoppel.
The judge made no order as to costs, criticising late disclosure and witness exaggeration by the company.
Seven months later the Earl applied out of time to appeal costs after a failed wasted costs application against the company's solicitors.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with extension of time against a no-order costs decision following trial of proprietary estoppel and licence issues.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; extension of time to argue other grounds set aside; respondents awarded 50% of appeal costs until 28 September 2004 and 100% thereafter.
enrichment.ratio: Where permission to appeal costs out of time was granted because a later wasted costs judgment appeared inconsistent, the court may limit the appeal to the changed circumstance; if that point fails there is no basis to disturb the original costs discretion or extend time for other grounds.
legal_issues: Whether the wasted costs judgment materially changed the judge's view on late disclosure
Whether extension of time should be granted to appeal a costs discretion
Whether the court could limit an appeal after granting permission on one ground
Appropriate costs order where only one of several grounds was argued

notes: Morris homelessness Article 14 challenge; Keith J declares section 185(4) Housing Act 1996 incompatible.

enrichment.short_title: Morris v Westminster: Article 14 challenge to homelessness priority need rules
key_facts: A British citizen from Mauritius with a dependent daughter subject to immigration control was refused priority need homelessness assistance by Westminster City Council.
The daughter later became a British citizen in June 2003; the claimant no longer needed personal relief but pursued the public law point with Crown intervention.
Section 185(4) required the council to disregard the child when determining the claimant's priority need because the child was ineligible for housing assistance.
The claim raised Article 14 discrimination in the enjoyment of Article 8 family life.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Substantive judicial review following earlier construction judgment, addressing Article 14, section 3 compatibility and section 4 declaration.
enrichment.outcome: Declaration of incompatibility made under section 4 HRA; section 185(4) could not be read compatibly under section 3; no further relief granted.
enrichment.ratio: Part VII homelessness provisions fall within the ambit of Article 8 because they promote family life; treating a British parent as lacking priority need solely because a dependent child is subject to immigration control is nationality discrimination that lacks objective and reasonable justification where section 185(4) is unlikely to achieve its stated anti-benefit-tourism aim.
legal_issues: Whether Part VII housing assistance falls within the ambit of Article 8
Whether section 185(4) discriminates on nationality against British citizen parents
Whether the discrimination pursues a legitimate aim proportionately
Whether section 185(4) can be read compatibly under section 3 HRA

notes: Planning enforcement appeal judicial review; Collins J quashes inspector decision on mixed-use change.

enrichment.short_title: Singh v First Secretary of State: planning enforcement appeal fairness
key_facts: Mr Singh carried on furniture manufacture, repair and retail at the Sofa Factory, Soho Hill, Birmingham, in a Grade II listed building purchased in 2000.
Previous occupiers Thomas A Ingram & Co had manufactured and retailed signs from the premises for over 30 years.
An enforcement notice dated 9 October 2003 alleged a material change to mixed manufacturing and retail use and required cessation of all retail sales within two months.
The appellant appealed on section 174(2)(b) grounds that the alleged breach had not occurred, relying on longstanding retail use evidence.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of a planning inspector's decision dismissing an enforcement notice appeal dealt with by written representations.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed and inspector's decision quashed; matter remitted for reconsideration with costs to the appellant subject to detailed assessment.
enrichment.ratio: On a section 174(2)(b) appeal the appellant bears the onus to show the alleged breach has not occurred; where advisers focus only on prior retail use because the notice prohibits all retail sales, an inspector must fairly consider whether present use is materially different from previous manufacturing-and-retail use and whether the notice requires excessive steps including forbidding ancillary retail sales.
legal_issues: Whether the inspector erred in treating ground (b) without adequate comparison of previous and current use
Burden of proof on enforcement appeal under Nelsovil
Whether previous retail use was ancillary or mixed use
Whether the notice improperly required cessation of all retail sales rather than non-ancillary retail only
linked_authorities: Nelsovil Ltd v Minister of Housing and Local Government [1962] 1 WLR 404

confidence.notes: Final quashing order and detailed reasoning on inspector fairness are clear though remitted merits remain open.
